findings.title: `items.Count` is the number of order lines, not the number of units, so a line with quantity 3 returns its full line total instead of the per-item price. This also reintroduces division by zero for an empty order; sum quantities and retain the existing zero guard.
findings.explanation: `items.Count` is the number of order lines, not the number of units, so a line with quantity 3 returns its full line total instead of the per-item price. This also reintroduces division by zero for an empty order; sum quantities and retain the existing zero guard.
findings.reason: Flags line 45 dividing by items.Count (lines, not quantities) and the empty-order division by zero, matching label #2.

findings.title: This changes the documented boundary from inclusive to exclusive: a subtotal exactly 500 now misses the extra 5% tier discount, even though the comment and requirement say 500 or more. Keep the inclusive comparison so the threshold behaves as described.
findings.explanation: This changes the documented boundary from inclusive to exclusive: a subtotal exactly 500 now misses the extra 5% tier discount, even though the comment and requirement say 500 or more. Keep the inclusive comparison so the threshold behaves as described.
findings.reason: Flags line 25 where a subtotal of exactly 500 misses the extra discount because the check is exclusive despite the 'or more' comment, matching label #1.

findings.title: Removing the allowlist check makes `sortBy` untrusted input flow directly into the interpolated SQL. A caller can inject expressions or terminate the `ORDER BY` clause, so this endpoint is now SQL-injection-prone. Restore the allowlist validation (and ideally use the matched canonical column name) before constructing the query.
findings.explanation: Removing the allowlist check makes `sortBy` untrusted input flow directly into the interpolated SQL. A caller can inject expressions or terminate the `ORDER BY` clause, so this endpoint is now SQL-injection-prone. Restore the allowlist validation (and ideally use the matched canonical column name) before constructing the query.
findings.reason: Describes cs-02-invoice-repository#1 but at lines 24-24, outside the window. Identifies SQL injection via unvalidated sortBy interpolated into the ORDER BY clause with the allowlist unused; the line is slightly off (24 vs 28) but it is the same defect.

findings.title: The connection is no longer disposed after the command completes. Even though `SqlConnection` uses pooling, failing to dispose it prevents the connection from being returned to the pool promptly and can exhaust the pool under repeated calls. Keep the `await using` declaration here.
findings.explanation: The connection is no longer disposed after the command completes. Even though `SqlConnection` uses pooling, failing to dispose it prevents the connection from being returned to the pool promptly and can exhaust the pool under repeated calls. Keep the `await using` declaration here.
findings.reason: Identifies the undisposed SqlConnection in DeleteOlderThanAsync, which can exhaust the connection pool.

findings.title: Using `Random` makes reset tokens predictable and reduces them to only six decimal digits, so an attacker can enumerate guesses or reproduce the generator state. Password-reset credentials need a cryptographically secure random value with substantially more entropy; retain the cryptographic byte generation used previously (or use an equivalent CSPRNG).
findings.explanation: Using `Random` makes reset tokens predictable and reduces them to only six decimal digits, so an attacker can enumerate guesses or reproduce the generator state. Password-reset credentials need a cryptographically secure random value with substantially more entropy; retain the cryptographic byte generation used previously (or use an equivalent CSPRNG).
findings.reason: Identifies the use of System.Random and the six-digit space on line 21 as predictable and guessable, and calls for a CSPRNG, matching label #1.

findings.title: This comparison rejects every unexpired token (`ExpiresAt` is normally in the future) and allows expired tokens to continue to the hash check. Reverse the comparison so redemption returns false only when the expiration is before the current time.
findings.explanation: This comparison rejects every unexpired token (`ExpiresAt` is normally in the future) and allows expired tokens to continue to the hash check. Reverse the comparison so redemption returns false only when the expiration is before the current time.
findings.reason: Identifies the inverted expiry comparison on line 29, where unexpired tokens are rejected and expired ones accepted, matching label #2.

findings.title: The stored file name now comes from `file.FileName`, which the client controls. A name such as `../../web.config` can escape the `uploads` folder and overwrite files under the content root, and repeated names overwrite earlier documents. Restore the GUID-based `storedName` so the server controls the file name. This change is required before merge.
findings.explanation: The stored file name now comes from `file.FileName`, which the client controls. A name such as `../../web.config` can escape the `uploads` folder and overwrite files under the content root, and repeated names overwrite earlier documents. Restore the GUID-based `storedName` so the server controls the file name. This change is required before merge.
findings.reason: Client-controlled file.FileName used as the stored name allows traversal out of the uploads folder and overwrites on duplicate names, which is exactly label #1.

findings.title: The path-traversal check was removed from `Download`, so `id` goes straight into `Path.Combine`. A value such as `../appsettings.json` can read files outside the `uploads` folder. Restore the check before building the path. The `Path.GetFileName(id) != id` test is a stricter guard that also rejects rooted values. This change is required before merge.
findings.explanation: The path-traversal check was removed from `Download`, so `id` goes straight into `Path.Combine`. A value such as `../appsettings.json` can read files outside the `uploads` folder. Restore the check before building the path. The `Path.GetFileName(id) != id` test is a stricter guard that also rejects rooted values. This change is required before merge.
findings.reason: Download passes id straight into Path.Combine with no check, allowing traversal or rooted paths, which is label #3.

findings.title: The upload now uses the synchronous `CopyTo` into a `MemoryStream`, then calls `ToArray()`, which makes a second full copy of the file. Large uploads use extra memory and block a thread-pool thread inside an async action, and `ct` is not honored during the copy. Restore streaming with `CopyToAsync(target, ct)` to avoid both problems.
findings.explanation: The upload now uses the synchronous `CopyTo` into a `MemoryStream`, then calls `ToArray()`, which makes a second full copy of the file. Large uploads use extra memory and block a thread-pool thread inside an async action, and `ct` is not honored during the copy. Restore streaming with `CopyToAsync(target, ct)` to avoid both problems.
findings.reason: Synchronous CopyTo into a MemoryStream followed by ToArray() buffers the whole upload in memory and blocks a thread instead of streaming, which is label #2.

findings.title: Changing this cache to a plain `Dictionary` makes concurrent calls unsafe: multiple requests can read and write `_rates` at the same time, and `Dictionary` does not support concurrent access (potential corruption or exceptions). Keep a thread-safe collection here, or protect every access with a lock.
findings.explanation: Changing this cache to a plain `Dictionary` makes concurrent calls unsafe: multiple requests can read and write `_rates` at the same time, and `Dictionary` does not support concurrent access (potential corruption or exceptions). Keep a thread-safe collection here, or protect every access with a lock.
findings.reason: Identifies the static plain Dictionary being accessed concurrently as unsafe, the same defect as label #1.

findings.title: `ConvertAsync` is already asynchronous, but `.Result` blocks its caller while the HTTP operation completes and can deadlock when this library is used under a synchronization context; it also defeats asynchronous scalability. Await the operation and propagate the cancellation/exception normally.
findings.explanation: `ConvertAsync` is already asynchronous, but `.Result` blocks its caller while the HTTP operation completes and can deadlock when this library is used under a synchronization context; it also defeats asynchronous scalability. Await the operation and propagate the cancellation/exception normally.
findings.reason: Identifies blocking .Result in async ConvertAsync with deadlock risk and a request to await instead, the same defect as label #2.

findings.title: This bound prevents the third and final attempt from ever running. With the current loop, a transient failure on attempt 2 falls through to `Unreachable` after the delay, and `MaxAttempts == 1` would make the method perform no request at all. Use an inclusive bound so the configured maximum is actually honored.
findings.explanation: This bound prevents the third and final attempt from ever running. With the current loop, a transient failure on attempt 2 falls through to `Unreachable` after the delay, and `MaxAttempts == 1` would make the method perform no request at all. Use an inclusive bound so the configured maximum is actually honored.
findings.reason: Identifies the off-by-one loop bound on line 13 that stops the final attempt and falls through to the 'Unreachable' exception.

findings.title: This bypasses the configured named `shipping` client used by the other method, so its BaseAddress, authentication/default headers, handlers, timeouts, and other transport settings are not applied to shipment requests. Creating and disposing a new `HttpClient` per call also prevents connection reuse under load. Obtain the client from `factory` instead.
findings.explanation: This bypasses the configured named `shipping` client used by the other method, so its BaseAddress, authentication/default headers, handlers, timeouts, and other transport settings are not applied to shipment requests. Creating and disposing a new `HttpClient` per call also prevents connection reuse under load. Obtain the client from `factory` instead.
findings.reason: Identifies the per-call new HttpClient on line 40 that bypasses the factory's 'shipping' client and prevents connection reuse.

findings.title: `to` is documented as inclusive, but using midnight at the start of `to` as the exclusive bound excludes every order placed on the end date (and makes a one-day range empty). Advance the bound by one day so the whole requested final date is included.
findings.explanation: `to` is documented as inclusive, but using midnight at the start of `to` as the exclusive bound excludes every order placed on the end date (and makes a one-day range empty). Advance the bound by one day so the whole requested final date is included.
findings.reason: Same defect: the end bound is midnight at the start of `to` with an exclusive filter, so the last day is excluded despite the inclusive documentation.

findings.title: This adds one `Customers` query for every distinct customer after the orders query, so report latency and database round trips grow linearly with the number of customers. Project the customer name and aggregate in the original EF query instead of loading groups and querying inside the loop.
findings.explanation: This adds one `Customers` query for every distinct customer after the orders query, so report latency and database round trips grow linearly with the number of customers. Project the customer name and aggregate in the original EF query instead of loading groups and querying inside the loop.
findings.reason: Same defect: one Customers query per group inside the loop (N+1). The category is labeled Bug rather than Performance, but the problem is identical.

findings.title: When a customer has no orders, `totals` is empty and `Average()` throws `InvalidOperationException`. The previous implementation returned `0m` for this case; keep that empty-result handling unless the API is intentionally changing its contract.
findings.explanation: When a customer has no orders, `totals` is empty and `Average()` throws `InvalidOperationException`. The previous implementation returned `0m` for this case; keep that empty-result handling unless the API is intentionally changing its contract.
findings.reason: Same defect: Average() on an empty sequence throws InvalidOperationException when a customer has no orders. The mention of a 'previous implementation' is extra, but the core issue is the same.

findings.title: Using a predictable fallback signing key means any deployment that omits `Jwt:SigningKey` will accept tokens signed with this publicly visible value, including in production. This changes the previous fail-fast behavior into an authentication bypass risk; keep the required configuration check (or reject startup when the key is missing) instead of supplying a shared default.
findings.explanation: Using a predictable fallback signing key means any deployment that omits `Jwt:SigningKey` will accept tokens signed with this publicly visible value, including in production. This changes the previous fail-fast behavior into an authentication bypass risk; keep the required configuration check (or reject startup when the key is missing) instead of supplying a shared default.
findings.reason: Flags the hardcoded fallback signing key on line 11 that lets deployments missing the setting accept tokens signed with a known value.

findings.title: Disabling lifetime validation allows expired tokens and tokens whose `nbf` is in the future to authenticate. `ClockSkew` cannot protect this path while `ValidateLifetime` is false; this should remain enabled for bearer authentication.
findings.explanation: Disabling lifetime validation allows expired tokens and tokens whose `nbf` is in the future to authenticate. `ClockSkew` cannot protect this path while `ValidateLifetime` is false; this should remain enabled for bearer authentication.
findings.reason: Flags ValidateLifetime = false on line 23, which lets expired tokens authenticate.

findings.title: `Authorization` contains the complete bearer credential, so including it in the authentication-failure log writes reusable access tokens to the logging system and any downstream sinks. Log the rejection reason without the header (or a deliberately non-reversible identifier) instead.
findings.explanation: `Authorization` contains the complete bearer credential, so including it in the authentication-failure log writes reusable access tokens to the logging system and any downstream sinks. Log the rejection reason without the header (or a deliberately non-reversible identifier) instead.
findings.reason: Flags the Authorization header written to the failure log on line 35, which exposes bearer tokens.

findings.title: `ExecuteNonQueryAsync` does not reliably return the number of rows updated here: `SET NOCOUNT ON` can make it return `-1`, and triggers can alter the reported count. In either case, a successful rename can be reported as `false` (and a trigger's row count can make a single-row update fail the `== 1` check). Return the affected-row count from the SQL batch (for example with `SELECT @@ROWCOUNT`) and read that scalar instead.
findings.explanation: `ExecuteNonQueryAsync` does not reliably return the number of rows updated here: `SET NOCOUNT ON` can make it return `-1`, and triggers can alter the reported count. In either case, a successful rename can be reported as `false` (and a trigger's row count can make a single-row update fail the `== 1` check). Return the affected-row count from the SQL batch (for example with `SELECT @@ROWCOUNT`) and read that scalar instead.
findings.reason: The SQL is a plain UPDATE with no NOCOUNT or triggers in this code. SET NOCOUNT ON would have to be set by the server or in the batch, and neither is the case here. Triggers are speculative, and the proposed SELECT @@ROWCOUNT workaround is itself affected by triggers. ExecuteNonQueryAsync returning the affected row count is standard, correct behavior for this UPDATE.

findings.title: With the default ASP.NET Core JWT bearer claim mapping, a token's `sub` claim is exposed as `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`, not as a literal `"sub"` claim. Valid authenticated callers can therefore hit this exception and receive a 500 instead of placing or reading an order. Read the mapped name-identifier claim (and optionally fall back to `"sub"` if mapping is disabled), or configure claim mapping consistently.
findings.explanation: With the default ASP.NET Core JWT bearer claim mapping, a token's `sub` claim is exposed as `ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`, not as a literal `"sub"` claim. Valid authenticated callers can therefore hit this exception and receive a 500 instead of placing or reading an order. Read the mapped name-identifier claim (and optionally fall back to `"sub"` if mapping is disabled), or configure claim mapping consistently.
findings.reason: The finding depends on JWT bearer claim-mapping configuration that is not in this file. Many apps disable inbound claim mapping (`MapInboundClaims = false`), and reading the literal `"sub"` claim is then correct. The file is labelled defect-free, and the claim that valid callers will get a 500 is speculative.

findings.title: Both `tableName` and `userId` are interpolated into SQL. A caller can inject SQL through either value, and `tableName` cannot be fixed with a parameter alone; allowlist table names and pass `userId` as a typed parameter before executing the query.
findings.explanation: Both `tableName` and `userId` are interpolated into SQL. A caller can inject SQL through either value, and `tableName` cannot be fixed with a parameter alone; allowlist table names and pass `userId` as a typed parameter before executing the query.
findings.reason: SQL injection via interpolated tableName and userId on line 26.

findings.title: Sensitive data is encrypted with obsolete DES using a hard-coded, publicly visible key and a fixed IV. This provides no meaningful confidentiality and identical plaintext blocks can produce repeatable ciphertext; use an approved authenticated-encryption scheme such as AES-GCM with a managed key and a fresh nonce per value.
findings.explanation: Sensitive data is encrypted with obsolete DES using a hard-coded, publicly visible key and a fixed IV. This provides no meaningful confidentiality and identical plaintext blocks can produce repeatable ciphertext; use an approved authenticated-encryption scheme such as AES-GCM with a managed key and a fresh nonce per value.
findings.reason: Covers both obsolete DES and the hardcoded key/fixed IV.

findings.title: `fileName` is directly appended to the base directory, so values containing `..\` or an absolute path can escape `C:\UserFiles` and disclose arbitrary readable files. Canonicalize the candidate path and reject anything outside the intended root (and reject rooted paths) before reading.
findings.explanation: `fileName` is directly appended to the base directory, so values containing `..\` or an absolute path can escape `C:\UserFiles` and disclose arbitrary readable files. Canonicalize the candidate path and reject anything outside the intended root (and reject rooted paths) before reading.
findings.reason: Path traversal through fileName in the path.

findings.title: The method passes an arbitrary caller-supplied string to `cmd.exe` with `/c`, which is direct command injection and allows execution with the service account's privileges. Do not invoke a shell with user input; expose a fixed operation/argument allowlist or remove this execution path.
findings.explanation: The method passes an arbitrary caller-supplied string to `cmd.exe` with `/c`, which is direct command injection and allows execution with the service account's privileges. Do not invoke a shell with user input; expose a fixed operation/argument allowlist or remove this execution path.
findings.reason: Command injection via cmd.exe /c with caller input.

findings.title: The comment is inserted into an HTML response without encoding. A comment containing markup or script will execute when the client renders `message`, creating a stored/reflected XSS path; HTML-encode the value or return the raw comment as data and let the view encode it.
findings.explanation: The comment is inserted into an HTML response without encoding. A comment containing markup or script will execute when the client renders `message`, creating a stored/reflected XSS path; HTML-encode the value or return the raw comment as data and let the view encode it.
findings.reason: XSS from unencoded comment in HTML.

findings.title: The authentication query compares the supplied password directly with a database column, so the system must retain a plaintext-equivalent password and sends the raw credential to SQL. Store a salted password hash and verify it in the application using a password-hashing API instead of querying on `Password = @password`.
findings.explanation: The authentication query compares the supplied password directly with a database column, so the system must retain a plaintext-equivalent password and sends the raw credential to SQL. Store a salted password hash and verify it in the application using a password-hashing API instead of querying on `Password = @password`.
findings.reason: Describes seed-01-user-data-service#10 but at lines 100-100, outside the window. Plaintext password comparison in query; line is slightly off but same defect.

findings.title: An authentication failure exception includes `ConnectionString`, which contains the database host and credential, in a message that can reach an API caller or be logged externally. Return a generic authentication error and keep connection details only in protected server-side diagnostics.
findings.explanation:
An authentication failure exception includes `ConnectionString`, which contains the database host and credential, in a message that can reach an API caller or be logged externally. Return a generic authentication error and keep connection details only in protected server-side diagnostics.

This issue also appears on line 113 of the same file.

findings.title: This response exposes the service's hard-coded API key to every caller that authenticates successfully. A server credential must not be returned as user data; remove it from the response and use a separately issued, scoped token only if the client actually needs one.
findings.explanation: This response exposes the service's hard-coded API key to every caller that authenticates successfully. A server credential must not be returned as user data; remove it from the response and use a separately issued, scoped token only if the client actually needs one.
findings.reason: API key returned to the caller on successful login.

findings.title: This loop creates one million files and allocates a `MemoryStream`, `FileStream`, and `HttpClient` per iteration without disposing any of them. It can exhaust file handles, sockets, and disk, and leaves the generated files behind; process data in bounded batches, reuse clients, dispose streams, and avoid unbounded file creation.
findings.explanation: This loop creates one million files and allocates a `MemoryStream`, `FileStream`, and `HttpClient` per iteration without disposing any of them. It can exhaust file handles, sockets, and disk, and leaves the generated files behind; process data in bounded batches, reuse clients, dispose streams, and avoid unbounded file creation.
findings.reason: Undisposed MemoryStream, FileStream and HttpClient created in a loop.

findings.title: Seeding `Random` with a constant makes every invocation return the same predictable token. This is not suitable for authentication or session material; fill the byte array with a cryptographic RNG such as `RandomNumberGenerator.Fill`.
findings.explanation: Seeding `Random` with a constant makes every invocation return the same predictable token. This is not suitable for authentication or session material; fill the byte array with a cryptographic RNG such as `RandomNumberGenerator.Fill`.
findings.reason: Constant-seeded Random used for a security token.

findings.title: This unused constant is another encryption secret committed to source control, while the encryption method below uses a different hard-coded DES key. Remove unused secret material and obtain any real encryption key from managed secret storage; keeping it here creates exposure without providing protection.
findings.explanation: This unused constant is another encryption secret committed to source control, while the encryption method below uses a different hard-coded DES key. Remove unused secret material and obtain any real encryption key from managed secret storage; keeping it here creates exposure without providing protection.
findings.reason: The hardcoded EncryptionKey on line 12 is a real secret committed to source and no label covers it. Label 6 covers only the key and IV on lines 44-45.

findings.title: The constructor opens a SqlConnection that the class never closes or disposes. Each service instance therefore retains a database connection until finalization, and repeated construction can exhaust the connection pool; acquire/close a connection per operation or implement deterministic disposal and manage the service lifetime accordingly.
findings.explanation: The constructor opens a SqlConnection that the class never closes or disposes. Each service instance therefore retains a database connection until finalization, and repeated construction can exhaust the connection pool; acquire/close a connection per operation or implement deterministic disposal and manage the service lifetime accordingly.
findings.reason: Connection opened in the constructor and never closed or disposed.

findings.title: The Process instance is never disposed. Repeated command requests can retain process-related OS resources; declare it with a `using` scope so it is disposed even when starting or reading the process fails.
findings.explanation: The Process instance is never disposed. Repeated command requests can retain process-related OS resources; declare it with a `using` scope so it is disposed even when starting or reading the process fails.
findings.reason: Process is not disposed; this is a genuine minor resource leak that no label covers.

findings.title: Untrusted comment text is written directly into a log entry, including any newline/control characters, so an attacker can forge additional log records; the missing line terminator also concatenates separate requests. Use structured logging (or sanitize control characters and append a delimiter) rather than interpolating the raw value.
findings.explanation: Untrusted comment text is written directly into a log entry, including any newline/control characters, so an attacker can forge additional log records; the missing line terminator also concatenates separate requests. Use structured logging (or sanitize control characters and append a delimiter) rather than interpolating the raw value.
findings.reason: Log forging through unsanitized comment text written to the log is a genuine issue that no label covers.

findings.title: The increment and return are not atomic. Concurrent callers can read and overwrite the same value, producing duplicate IDs; replace the increment/sleep sequence with an atomic operation such as `Interlocked.Increment(ref _counter)`.
findings.explanation: The increment and return are not atomic. Concurrent callers can read and overwrite the same value, producing duplicate IDs; replace the increment/sleep sequence with an atomic operation such as `Interlocked.Increment(ref _counter)`.
findings.reason: Non-atomic increment of the shared static counter.

findings.title: This import references `UserDashboard.module.css`, but that file is not present in the repository snapshot or this change, so module resolution will fail and the component cannot build. Add the stylesheet (and its module declarations if required) or remove the import and class usage.
findings.explanation: This import references `UserDashboard.module.css`, but that file is not present in the repository snapshot or this change, so module resolution will fail and the component cannot build. Add the stylesheet (and its module declarations if required) or remove the import and class usage.

findings.title: This inserts the user-controlled name as HTML, so a name such as an image with an event handler can execute script in the dashboard. Render the value as React text or sanitize it with a strict, trusted allowlist.
findings.explanation: This inserts the user-controlled name as HTML, so a name such as an image with an event handler can execute script in the dashboard. Render the value as React text or sanitize it with a strict, trusted allowlist.

findings.title: The browser receives a bearer API key and an admin password and sends them over plain HTTP. Anyone who inspects the bundle or network can impersonate the admin; keep privileged access server-side, use scoped short-lived credentials, and require HTTPS.
findings.explanation:
The browser receives a bearer API key and an admin password and sends them over plain HTTP. Anyone who inspects the bundle or network can impersonate the admin; keep privileged access server-side, use scoped short-lived credentials, and require HTTPS.

This issue also appears on line 34 of the same file.

findings.title: Passwords and the API key are persisted in `localStorage`, which is readable by any script running in the origin and commonly exposed by XSS or browser extensions. Do not store credentials client-side; use a server-managed session and keep only non-sensitive display data in browser storage.
findings.explanation: Passwords and the API key are persisted in `localStorage`, which is readable by any script running in the origin and commonly exposed by XSS or browser extensions. Do not store credentials client-side; use a server-managed session and keep only non-sensitive display data in browser storage.
findings.reason: Covers passwords and the API key stored in localStorage.

findings.title: If any record lacks a name, `processed` is never incremented and this loop spins on the browser's main thread indefinitely. The sample records added below do lack `name`; handle invalid records while still advancing the cursor.
findings.explanation: If any record lacks a name, `processed` is never incremented and this loop spins on the browser's main thread indefinitely. The sample records added below do lack `name`; handle invalid records while still advancing the cursor.

findings.title: A single click allocates one million objects and builds a roughly multi-gigabyte repeated string for each object. This can freeze or crash the browser and is an unbounded client-side memory spike; cap or paginate sample data and avoid materializing it all at once.
findings.explanation: A single click allocates one million objects and builds a roughly multi-gigabyte repeated string for each object. This can freeze or crash the browser and is an unbounded client-side memory spike; cap or paginate sample data and avoid materializing it all at once.
findings.reason: Describes seed-02-user-dashboard#11 but at lines 106-106, outside the window. A million large objects built in one click, causing a freeze and memory exhaustion.

findings.title: These records are appended to `User[]` even though they have `data`/`metadata` but no required `name` or `email`. That either makes the TypeScript update fail or leaves malformed users that later rendering, searching, and refresh logic cannot handle; keep sample records separate or construct valid `User` objects.
findings.explanation: These records are appended to `User[]` even though they have `data`/`metadata` but no required `name` or `email`. findings.reason: The sample objects are appended to User[] without name or email, producing malformed users that later code does not handle. This is a genuine type and data defect not covered by any label.

findings.title: `eval` executes arbitrary JavaScript in the page context. The Enter handler passes raw input here, and the greeting path interpolates a user name, allowing code to read `localStorage` and perform actions as the user; remove `eval` and implement explicit, non-code behavior instead.
findings.explanation: `eval` executes arbitrary JavaScript in the page context. The Enter handler passes raw input here, and the greeting path interpolates a user name, allowing code to read `localStorage` and perform actions as the user; remove `eval` and implement explicit, non-code behavior instead.

findings.title: This renders passwords and full credit-card values into the DOM. Anyone with dashboard access or DOM access can view the secrets; never render passwords and show only a masked/tokenized card value after enforcing the appropriate authorization.
findings.explanation: This renders passwords and full credit-card values into the DOM. Anyone with dashboard access or DOM access can view the secrets; never render passwords and show only a masked/tokenized card value after enforcing the appropriate authorization.
findings.reason: Passwords and credit card numbers rendered into the DOM.

findings.title: The interval is never cleared when the component unmounts. Each mount leaves a timer logging forever, and repeated mounts accumulate timers; return a cleanup function that calls `clearInterval`.
findings.explanation: The interval is never cleared when the component unmounts. Each mount leaves a timer logging forever, and repeated mounts accumulate timers; return a cleanup function that calls `clearInterval`.

findings.title: This filters the current `users` state and then replaces it, so each keystroke searches an already-filtered subset and clearing the input cannot restore the original results. Keep the unfiltered collection separately and derive the displayed list from the current term.
findings.explanation: This filters the current `users` state and then replaces it, so each keystroke searches an already-filtered subset and clearing the input cannot restore the original results. Keep the unfiltered collection separately and derive the displayed list from the current term.

findings.title: Because the async function neither awaits nor returns this `Promise.all`, it resolves before any refresh finishes and rejected requests become unhandled promise rejections. Await the batch and handle or propagate its failure so the caller can observe refresh errors.
findings.explanation: Because the async function neither awaits nor returns this `Promise.all`, it resolves before any refresh finishes and rejected requests become unhandled promise rejections. Await the batch and handle or propagate its failure so the caller can observe refresh errors.

findings.title: The balance is read with a plain `SELECT`, and the debit writes an absolute value (`@Balance - @Amount`). AND Balance >= @Amount` and check `@@ROWCOUNT`, so the check and the debit happen in one statement.
findings.explanation: The balance is read with a plain `SELECT`, and the debit writes an absolute value (`@Balance - @Amount`). findings.reason: Describes the unlocked read followed by an absolute-value write that lets concurrent transfers overdraw the account and lose a debit, which is label #1. The reported line is slightly off but the code is the same.

findings.title: `NOT IN` is null-sensitive: if any order has a NULL `CustomerId`, the subquery contains NULL and this predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN for every customer, so the procedure returns no rows rather than the customers without orders. Use a correlated `NOT EXISTS` (as in the previous implementation) so unrelated NULL customer IDs do not affect the result.
findings.reason: Describes the NOT IN NULL-sensitivity problem, where a NULL CustomerId makes the procedure return no rows, and recommends NOT EXISTS. The reported line is slightly off, but the defect is the same.

findings.title: Applying `YEAR` to `o.OrderDate` makes the predicate non-sargable, so SQL Server cannot efficiently seek an index on `OrderDate` and may scan the entire Orders table for every execution. findings.reason: Describes YEAR() on OrderDate making the filter non-sargable and recommends a half-open date range, the same defect as the label on line 12.

findings.title: Switching from `SCOPE_IDENTITY()` to `@@IDENTITY` is a regression. `@@IDENTITY` returns the last identity value generated in the session by any scope, including triggers on `dbo.ImportLog`, so `@LogId` can point at the wrong log row. Those rows are then used to stamp `staging.PriceChanges.ImportLogId`. `SCOPE_IDENTITY()` limits the value to the current scope, which is what this code needs. Restore it.

findings.reason: Identifies @@IDENTITY on line 28 returning an identity from another scope (e.g. a trigger) and recommends SCOPE_IDENTITY().

findings.title: The set-based `UPDATE ... FROM ... JOIN` was replaced with a row-by-row cursor that runs one UPDATE per staged row. For large batches this adds statement overhead, round trips, and log writes, and it holds locks longer inside the transaction, with no clear gain. Restore the set-based update, which returns the same `@@ROWCOUNT`. If the cursor is required for a documented reason, declare it `LOCAL` (for example, `DECLARE changes CURSOR LOCAL FAST_FORWARD FOR`) so it is released when the procedure exits; a `GLOBAL` cursor can stay allocated after an error and cause a "cursor already exists" error on the next call. This change is mandatory unless the cursor is needed for a documented reason. If duplicate SKUs can appear in a batch, handle them explicitly, because the set-based update applies an arbitrary match in that case.
findings.explanation: The set-based `UPDATE ... FROM ... JOIN` was replaced with a row-by-row cursor that runs one UPDATE per staged row. For large batches this adds statement overhead, round trips, and log writes, and it holds locks longer inside the transaction, with no clear gain. Restore the set-based update, which returns the same `@@ROWCOUNT`. This change is mandatory unless the cursor is needed for a documented reason. If duplicate SKUs can appear in a batch, handle them explicitly, because the set-based update applies an arbitrary match in that case.
findings.reason: Identifies the row-by-row cursor update inside the transaction as slow and lock-holding, and recommends a set-based UPDATE with a join. The line is at the end of the cursor block, which is close enough.

findings.title: `SELECT ... INTO @CustomerId` does not assign `NULL` when no row matches; it leaves the output parameter's incoming value unchanged. If a caller reuses a non-NULL variable, a new email therefore skips the insert and updates that unrelated `CustomerId` (or returns the stale ID). Reset `@CustomerId` before this lookup, or use a local variable initialized to `NULL` for the lookup result.
findings.explanation: `SELECT ... INTO @CustomerId` does not assign `NULL` when no row matches; it leaves the output parameter's incoming value unchanged. If a caller reuses a non-NULL variable, a new email therefore skips the insert and updates that unrelated `CustomerId` (or returns the stale ID). Reset `@CustomerId` before this lookup, or use a local variable initialized to `NULL` for the lookup result.
findings.reason: The bug is genuine. In T-SQL, `SELECT @var = col` with no matching row leaves the variable unchanged, and an OUTPUT parameter also carries its incoming value. A caller that passes in a non-NULL `@CustomerId` would skip the insert and update an unrelated customer. The finding's wording "SELECT ... INTO" is slightly off, but the defect it describes is correct. No label covers it.

findings.title: `NULL` bypasses this `NOT BETWEEN` check because the predicate evaluates to `UNKNOWN`; the procedure then builds a null date range and silently returns no rows instead of rejecting an invalid year. Include an explicit null check in the validation condition.
findings.explanation: `NULL` bypasses this `NOT BETWEEN` check because the predicate evaluates to `UNKNOWN`; the procedure then builds a null date range and silently returns no rows instead of rejecting an invalid year. Include an explicit null check in the validation condition.
findings.reason: Correct: with @Year NULL, `NULL NOT BETWEEN ...` is UNKNOWN so THROW is skipped. DATEFROMPARTS(NULL,...) returns NULL, the filters are UNKNOWN and no rows come back, so an invalid NULL year is silently accepted rather than rejected.

findings.title: The search term is no longer passed through `encodeURIComponent` in the fetch URL. Reserved characters such as `&`, `#`, `+`, and `=` change the request: `a&limit=1000` adds a parameter, `#` truncates the query, and `+` is decoded as a space. This can return wrong results and lets users add extra parameters to the API request. Restore `encodeURIComponent(term)`. This change is mandatory.
findings.explanation: The search term is no longer passed through `encodeURIComponent` in the fetch URL. findings.reason: Reports the unencoded search term in the fetch URL, where reserved characters like & and # break the query string; same as label 2.

findings.title: `Date` uses zero-based month indexes, while `CalendarDay.month` is documented as 1–12. Passing `month` directly makes every conversion one month late (and month 12 roll over into the next year), so `toDate({ year: 2026, month: 1, day: 1 })` becomes February 1. Subtract one before passing the month to the constructor.
findings.explanation: `Date` uses zero-based month indexes, while `CalendarDay.month` is documented as 1–12. Passing `month` directly makes every conversion one month late (and month 12 roll over into the next year), so `toDate({ year: 2026, month: 1, day: 1 })` becomes February 1. Subtract one before passing the month to the constructor.
findings.reason: Identifies that toDate passes the 1-based month directly to the Date constructor, which expects 0-based months, so every date is one month late.

findings.title: `getDay()` returns the weekday number (0–6), not the day of the month. This makes `fromDate` return values such as `day: 0` for Sundays, and causes `addDays` to produce invalid calendar-day results. Use `getDate()` for the 1–31 calendar day.
findings.explanation: `getDay()` returns the weekday number (0–6), not the day of the month. This makes `fromDate` return values such as `day: 0` for Sundays, and causes `addDays` to produce invalid calendar-day results. Use `getDate()` for the 1–31 calendar day.
findings.reason: Identifies that fromDate uses getDay() (weekday) instead of getDate() (day of month).

findings.title: `Number.isSafeInteger` only guarantees that the cent count itself is exact; dividing it by 100 can still round away the cent before `Intl.NumberFormat` sees it. For example, `formatCents(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, "USD", "en-US")` formats the same as `formatCents(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER - 1, ...)` (`$90,071,992,547,409.90`), although the first amount should end in `.91`. Preserve the cent remainder when formatting (or reject values outside a documented precisely representable range) instead of passing `cents / 100` directly.
findings.explanation: `Number.isSafeInteger` only guarantees that the cent count itself is exact; dividing it by 100 can still round away the cent before `Intl.NumberFormat` sees it. For example, `formatCents(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, "USD", "en-US")` formats the same as `formatCents(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER - 1, ...)` (`$90,071,992,547,409.90`), although the first amount should end in `.91`. Preserve the cent remainder when formatting (or reject values outside a documented precisely representable range) instead of passing `cents / 100` directly.
findings.reason: The precision loss only appears near 9e13 dollars. The stated example is also wrong: both MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and MAX_SAFE_INTEGER-1 divide to the same double (about .90625), so both format as .91, not .90. It is not a defect worth fixing in practice.

findings.title: `Number.isInteger` is true for values such as `1e20`, even though they are not safe integers. Such a `parts` value passes validation and is then used as the `Array.from` length, causing an invalid-length/allocation failure instead of the documented input `RangeError` and potentially creating an avoidable resource issue. Validate `parts` as a safe integer and apply an appropriate upper bound for the returned array.
findings.explanation: `Number.isInteger` is true for values such as `1e20`, even though they are not safe integers. Such a `parts` value passes validation and is then used as the `Array.from` length, causing an invalid-length/allocation failure instead of the documented input `RangeError` and potentially creating an avoidable resource issue. Validate `parts` as a safe integer and apply an appropriate upper bound for the returned array.
findings.reason: For a value like 1e20, Array.from with that length still throws a RangeError (invalid array length), so the failure is not unexpected. Large but valid lengths are a caller concern, so the rest is speculative advice.

findings.title: `Number.isSafeInteger` still permits `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, but multiplying the floored quotient by `parts` can leave the safe-integer range for a negative total. For example, `splitCents(-9007199254740991, 3)` computes `remainder` as 1 and returns values whose sum is `-9007199254740992`, violating the documented invariant. Compute the remainder with integer remainder arithmetic (or use `BigInt`) rather than reconstructing it via `base * parts`.
findings.explanation: `Number.isSafeInteger` still permits `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, but multiplying the floored quotient by `parts` can leave the safe-integer range for a negative total. For example, `splitCents(-9007199254740991, 3)` computes `remainder` as 1 and returns values whose sum is `-9007199254740992`, violating the documented invariant. Compute the remainder with integer remainder arithmetic (or use `BigInt`) rather than reconstructing it via `base * parts`.
findings.reason: For total=-9007199254740991 and parts=3, base*parts is -9007199254740993, which is not a safe integer and rounds to -9007199254740992. The remainder comes out as 1 instead of 2, so the parts do not sum to the total and the documented invariant breaks. The validation lets this input through, so it is a genuine edge-case bug.

findings.title: `crypto.randomUUID()` is not available in every runtime this component can execute in (notably non-secure browser contexts and many SSR/test environments). In those environments submitting the form throws before `setTodos`, so the advertised add action is completely broken. Use an ID generator supported by the application's runtime or a guarded fallback instead of calling this API unconditionally.
findings.explanation: `crypto.randomUUID()` is not available in every runtime this component can execute in (notably non-secure browser contexts and many SSR/test environments). In those environments submitting the form throws before `setTodos`, so the advertised add action is completely broken. Use an ID generator supported by the application's runtime or a guarded fallback instead of calling this API unconditionally.
findings.reason: The code calls crypto.randomUUID() inside an event handler, so it never runs during SSR. It is supported in all modern browsers and in current Node and jsdom. It only fails in non-secure contexts or very old runtimes, so the claim that add is broken is speculative. It is not a defect in this code.
